newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: FEATURE-Gulf arms salesmen say not merchants of death.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Gulf arms salesmen say not merchants of death.

text.p: Jorn Edgren, marketing director of Finnish company Golden Gun, was at his stand at Abu Dhabi's arms show last week explaining how he lures potential customers to a row of JatiMatic submachine guns.

"I look for people who look like they may be interested in submachine guns and I grab one of the guns and go out and stand in front of them," he said after fielding questions from two Ukranians peering through gun sights.
"I try to get the attention of decision-makers, like generals, and at the same time, we try to find people here who can network for us."
In another section of the IDEX arms show -- one of the world's biggest -- Fuat Tigin, an engineer who hoped his Arabic-speaking skills would help secure deals, explained the Turkish approach.
"Turkey is trying to penetrate the Gulf market but the Russians and Americans don't want us to. The only thing is to tell customers we offer lower prices," he said.
NO MENTION OF DEATH
During the arms show, every word except "death" was used to describe the lethal firepower delivered from a vast array of weapons on display -- from Howitzers to tanks to small pistols.
Arms dealers from around the world who gathered in Abu Dhabi to show off their tanks, missiles, pistols and other instruments of destruction each had their own strategy.
But, generally, the expensive and delicate art of selling weapons was couched in terms such as defence and "taking out your target".
"You can't really call us 'merchants of death'," said one American executive. "Countries have to defend themselves. This is a necessary evil."
Even the names of some of the weapons would have led you to believe that you were at the Olympics, not an oil-rich capital that had lured the big names in the international arms bazaar.
Taking a stroll along one of the exhibition areas you came across the Javelin -- but not the kind hurled by athletes.
It was an anti-tank weapons system that can hit the thinly armoured area around a tank's latch from two km (about a mile) away.
"This can destroy any tank. It is the wave of the future," said a salesman. "This is the best system of its kind in the world."
Nearby, a man in camouflage uniform fired a pistol at attackers crawling through desert scrub on an electronic screen.
Women in veils, and a smartly dressed Libyan man with slicked-back hair and a video recorder looked on as crowds stopped to study hit ratios.
ALL ACTIVITIES ARE OFFICIALLY SANCTIONED

All the activities were officially sanctioned by the more than 50 defence ministers who visited IDEX to back their companies and salute the handful of powerful men who give the green light on arms deals in Abu Dhabi.
Most of the serious business talk was done in lavish chalets on the edge of the IDEX site, where executives exchanged ideas and business cards and greeted diplomats.
Industry executives had speculated the UAE would award a $6 billion deal to supply up to 80 warplanes during the show.
They said turnout was strong but the show was an anti-climax in terms of deals signed -- from naval torpedoes to radar.
But there were light moments.
"We have a special device in this vehicle which actually allows you to see through people's clothes," said one engineer.
All the talk of lucrative arms deals even grabbed the attention of those who say they are opposed to weapons production on religious grounds.

"Thailand is a Buddhist country. Making weapons is offensive. But we came here to try to attract people to our defence exhibition later this year," said Gilbert Foong, managing director of "Thai '97", scheduled for October.
